title: Acid and Base Models: Arrhenius to Brønsted-Lowry | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module6/lesson01.sa

Ammonia turns litmus blue, but it has no hydroxide. Follow how the definition of an acid changed: Lavoisier's oxygen, Davy's hydrogen, Arrhenius's ions in water, and Brønsted-Lowry proton transfer. See why each model was replaced, where the hydroxide in ammonia solution really comes from, how an acid and a base react as gases, with no aqueous solution, and the limit even Brønsted-Lowry has. title: How Mutation Adds a New Allele to a Population | Year 12 Biology Module 6
description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module6/lesson01

Did penicillin make bacteria resistant, or was resistance already there? Starting from Alexander Fleming's 1945 warning, see how one changed base in one cell becomes a new allele in a population's gene pool. Learn how that allele is passed on in bacteria and animals, why mutation is random with respect to need, what replica plates show, and how antibiotics select. Compare mutation with meiosis, fertilisation and gene flow. Two exam-style questions include brief feedback.

description:

The same BRCA1 mutation can be in every cell of your body, or in just one. Why can only one of those be inherited? description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module6/lesson07

title: Enthalpy of Neutralisation Calculations: q = mcΔT to kJ/mol | Year 12 Chemistry
description:

Mixing hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide gives no fizz, but the temperature climbs. See why neutralisation releases heat (only hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions react; the other ions are spectators), why ΔH is negative, and why the enthalpy of neutralisation is quoted per mole of water. Then work through calorimetry calculations step by step: q = mcΔT with the total mass, moles of water from the reactant that runs out, including sulfuric acid, and ΔH = −q/n in kJ/mol. title: Why Weak Acids Release Different Heat in Neutralisation | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module6/lesson10.sa

Swap hydrochloric acid for a weak acid and you might expect less heat. Ethanoic acid gives almost the same enthalpy of neutralisation, and hydrofluoric acid gives more. See why: a weak acid still reacts completely, but it adds an ionisation step, and that step can absorb or release energy. Use Hess's law and a particle model to explain ethanoic acid, hydrofluoric acid and ammonia, then see why neutralisation heat cannot tell you how strong an acid is. Two exam-style questions at the end.

A CRISPR treatment for sickle cell disease is already approved, and headlines promise much more. See how CRISPR finds and cuts its target, how the sickle cell treatment switches foetal haemoglobin back on, and why working in a trial isn't the same as being available to everyone. Then follow a proposed future use, a gene drive against malaria mosquitoes: how it spreads to nearly all offspring, what lab cages showed, and what is still unknown. Learn to judge any future use by need, feasibility and fairness, and to write "could, if". Two exam-style questions with brief feedback.

title: How Can Biotechnology Change Biodiversity? Bananas, Rhinos and the Three Levels | Year 12 Biology
description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12/module6/lesson11.sa

A disease-resistant banana and a rescue plan for the northern white rhino both use genetic techniques to stop something dying out. But does either one increase biodiversity? Learn to trace an effect at three levels (genetic, species and ecosystem) and to name your baseline: compared with what? See why a resistant Cavendish is still one clone, how crop biotechnology can raise or lower species diversity in a field, and why rhino embryos from one female's eggs start a genetic bottleneck. Two exam-style questions with brief feedback.

description:

Year 12 Biology: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12

Judgement verbs carry many of the biggest questions in recent HSC Chemistry and Biology papers, and NESA's marking feedback often flags judgements made without enough reasons from the evidence. Learn what analyse, assess, evaluate and justify each ask for, how assess differs from evaluate, and the three parts an assess or evaluate answer needs: a verdict, the criteria you judge by, and evidence from the question for each. See a weak and a strong answer to an HSC-style evaluate question, then try two training questions, one in Chemistry and one in Biology.
